planting.note: Divide and plant clumps in spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled to full shade; this Himalayan relative of Liriope and Ophiopogon forms slow-spreading evergreen tufts best used as a woodland-floor companion rather than a fast groundcover.

directions: Theropogon pallidus is a little-grown, monotypic Himalayan genus closely related to Liriope and Ophiopogon, forming clumps of narrow, grass-like evergreen foliage from a short rhizome. In late spring to early summer it sends up short spikes of small, nodding, pale pink-and-white bellflowers, followed by blue-black berries similar to its mondo-grass relatives. It is slower to spread than Liriope and best suited to a shaded woodland edge or rock garden where its subtlety can be appreciated up close rather than used as a bold groundcover.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-5 inches deep in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in light, dappled shade; foliage emerges in autumn and overwinters, so choose a site sheltered from the coldest exposure.

directions: Native to the northwestern Himalaya and Afghanistan, Notholirion thomsonianum produces strap-shaped leaves in autumn that persist through winter before the bulb sends up a tall spike of fragrant, pale lilac-pink trumpet flowers in late spring. Like its lily relatives, the flowering bulb is monocarpic, exhausting itself after bloom, but it compensates by producing a cluster of offset bulbs around the base that carry the planting forward. Grow it at a woodland edge with excellent drainage and some shelter from harsh winter sun, which can scorch the overwintering foliage.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a lightly shaded woodland edge or alpine bed; the small bulbils that form along the flowering stem can be collected and grown on separately.

directions: Found at high elevation in the eastern Himalaya and southwestern China, Notholirion bulbuliferum carries dense spikes of funnel-shaped, pinkish-purple flowers on tall stems above a basal rosette of strap leaves. As its name suggests, the flowering stem characteristically produces small bulbils in the leaf axils, giving the species an easy vegetative route to increase even though, like other Notholirion, the parent bulb dies after flowering. It performs best in a cool, humus-rich woodland-edge bed with reliable moisture during growth and sharp drainage through winter dormancy.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil at a shaded woodland margin; this species resents hot, dry summers and performs best in climates with cool summer nights.

directions: A relative of Lilium from the alpine meadows and open woodland of the eastern Himalaya and southwestern China, Nomocharis aperta produces broad, saucer-shaped, pale pink to rose flowers with maroon spotting toward the center, held above whorled lance-shaped leaves. It is notoriously fussy outside cool, moist climates, demanding a humus-rich, free-draining woodland soil that never fully dries and summer temperatures on the cooler side. Gardeners in the Pacific Northwest, the British Isles, and similar cool-summer regions have the best success growing it at a lightly shaded woodland edge among ferns and other moisture-loving companions.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated corms in spring in acidic, moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade, ideally near the margin of a bog garden or shaded seep; this tiny native orchid depends on mycorrhizal fungi and resents disturbance.

directions: Green adder's-mouth orchid is a diminutive native terrestrial orchid found across much of eastern and central North America in acidic bogs, seeps, and moist deciduous woods, where a single rounded leaf clasps the base of a slender stem topped by a twisted spike of tiny, greenish, upside-down flowers in summer. Its small size and subtle coloring make it easy to overlook, but it rewards close inspection in a shaded native bog or fern garden with reliably moist, acidic soil. Like most terrestrial orchids it depends on specific soil fungi and establishes slowly, so site it in an undisturbed, consistently damp spot and leave it undisturbed for years.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade, similar to the siting used for hardy Calanthe and Bletilla; allow a season to establish before expecting bloom.

directions: Cremastra appendiculata is a hardy terrestrial orchid native to woodlands across Japan, Korea, China, and the Himalaya, growing from a cluster of rounded pseudobulbs that give rise to broad, pleated, lily-like leaves. In spring it sends up a slender arching spike of nodding, tubular, maroon-brown flowers with a faint garlicky scent, a quirk that accounts for one of its common names. It pairs naturally with hardy Calanthe and Bletilla in a shaded woodland bed, favoring the same moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil and slow, clump-forming growth habit.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated pseudobulb divisions in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full shade; this is a conservation-notable Chinese endemic and wild material should never be collected.

directions: Changnienia amoena is the sole species in its genus, a rare spring-flowering terrestrial orchid endemic to broadleaf and mixed forests in central and eastern China. Each pseudobulb produces a single broad, heart-shaped leaf and one large, showy, pale pink-to-lavender flower that opens in very early spring before the leaf has fully expanded, a sequence shared with some Erythronium and Cypripedium relatives in the same woodland niche. Listed as near-threatened in its native range due to habitat loss and overcollection, it is grown almost exclusively by specialist woodland-orchid collectors and botanical gardens working from nursery-propagated stock in cool, shaded, humus-rich beds.

planting.note: Plant small tubers in spring in a shallow pan or shaded rock-garden crevice filled with moisture-retentive, well-drained mix of leaf mold, grit, and moss; this diminutive Japanese orchid is a favorite subject for kusamono and bonsai companion plantings.

directions: Amitostigma keiskei is a tiny hardy terrestrial orchid native to mossy rock faces and cliff ledges in Japan, producing a cluster of small tubers from which thread-like leaves and short spikes of delicate pink flowers emerge in summer. Its minute scale and tolerance of shallow, well-drained mossy pockets have made it a long-standing favorite among Japanese alpine and kusamono enthusiasts, who grow it in shallow pans alongside dwarf ferns and mosses. Give it bright shade, a gritty but moisture-retentive mix, and protection from winter wet, and clumps will slowly offset into an increasingly showy summer display.

planting.note: Plant small tubers in spring in a shallow, well-drained pot or shaded garden pocket filled with a moisture-retentive, humus-rich mix; keep noticeably drier and cooler during the dormant winter rest.

directions: Native to grassy slopes and open woodland in Japan, Korea, and China, Ponerorchis graminifolia is a small, grass-leaved terrestrial orchid grown from tiny tubers that produce slender stems topped by a few showy pink, purple, or white flowers in late spring to early summer. It has long been a staple of Japanese hobbyist orchid culture, traditionally grown in shallow ceramic pots where generations of selection have produced an enormous range of flower forms and colors from this single wild species. In the garden it wants bright, dappled shade and reliably moist but well-drained soil through the growing season, followed by a cooler, drier winter dormancy.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade; it associates well with hardy Calanthe, Cremastra, and Bletilla in a shaded orchid bed.

directions: Oreorchis patens is a hardy terrestrial orchid distributed through the woodlands of Japan, Korea, China, and the Russian Far East, growing from a chain of rounded pseudobulbs that send up narrow, pleated leaves each spring. Slender, upright flower spikes carry a loose cluster of small, yellow-brown flowers often marked with purple-brown veining, blooming in late spring to early summer against the woodland floor's dappled light. It is an unassuming but reliably perennial companion for other hardy terrestrial orchids in a shaded, humus-rich bed, slowly building into a larger clump over successive seasons.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Japanese woodland species slowly spreads by rhizome to form a low, airy groundcover.

directions: Patrinia triloba is a shade-tolerant Japanese woodland perennial related to the taller, sun-loving Patrinia scabiosifolia, distinguished by its three-lobed, maple-like leaves and lower, more spreading habit. From late summer into fall it produces loose, airy clusters of small, bright golden-yellow flowers held just above the foliage on wiry stems, adding late-season color to shaded beds that have usually finished their main floral display by then. It spreads gently by rhizome to form an attractive, low groundcover under deciduous trees, tolerating the dry shade and root competition typical of a woodland garden once established.
